title: AI Ops Engineer
tagline: The person who makes sure AI can ship on Tuesday, break on Wednesday without taking the bank down, and prove to an auditor on Friday exactly what changed and why.
overview: This role is not a data scientist and not a classic DevOps engineer — it's the person who builds the paved road that lets application teams ship AI features (chatbots, copilots, agents, RAG pipelines) into a regulated bank without every team reinventing release safety from scratch. A bank needs this function because AI systems break the assumptions traditional CI/CD was built on: outputs are non-deterministic, quality can't be checked with a simple pass/fail test, cost scales with usage in ways finance can't forecast, and regulators expect the same evidentiary trail for a prompt change that they'd expect for a code change to a credit decisioning model. Interviewers are really probing three things: can you talk concretely about mechanics (not just buzzwords — actual pipeline stages, actual rollback triggers, actual token-cost dashboards), do you understand why AI release engineering differs from standard software CI/CD, and can you operate credibly inside a bank's control environment (change advisory boards, segregation of duties, audit evidence) without becoming the person who slows everything down. A strong candidate frames their experience as bridging two worlds — production engineering discipline and AI-specific lifecycle awareness — and gives specific, falsifiable examples (a pipeline they built, an incident they rolled back, a cost anomaly they caught) rather than describing LLMOps in the abstract. It also helps to acknowledge current reality: regulatory guidance on gen AI/agentic AI model risk is still catching up (the 2026 interagency guidance explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from its scope pending further rulemaking), so banks are building their own interim governance discipline — this role is often the one filling that gap in practice.

sections.heading: AI Release Engineering & Promotion Pipelines
sections.summary: Covers how release pipelines for AI apps, agents, and platform config differ from ordinary app CI/CD, and how to design promotion controls (dev → test → UAT → prod) that produce audit-ready evidence.

content.text: In a bank, an AI release pipeline has to move more than application code: it promotes prompts, model/version pins, retrieval indexes, guardrail configs, agent tool definitions, and evaluation datasets — each of which needs its own versioning and diffing, because a prompt edit or a model version bump can change behavior as much as a code change does. The core design pattern is the same promotion backbone used for infrastructure-as-code, extended with AI-specific gates: unit tests and static checks first, then an automated evaluation suite (accuracy/groundedness/safety scores against a golden dataset) as a required gate before a build is allowed into UAT, then a human/CAB-style approval gate before production promotion, with every gate emitting a signed artifact (test report, eval report, approver identity, timestamp) that becomes release evidence for audit and model risk teams.

items: Environment gating: GitHub Environments (dev/test/uat/prod) with required reviewers, wait timers, and branch/tag protection so only an approved, tagged build can reach a protected environment.

OIDC federated identity instead of long-lived cloud secrets — each environment's deploy job requests a short-lived token scoped to repo + branch + environment claims, so a compromised workflow in dev can't touch prod credentials.
Immutable artifact promotion: build once, promote the same container/image/config bundle through environments (never rebuild per-environment) so what was tested is what ships.
Config-as-code for prompts, model routing, and guardrail thresholds, stored and reviewed the same way as application code (PR + review + diff), not edited live in a vendor console.

Release evidence bundle auto-generated per promotion: eval scores, security scan results, SBOM, approver list, and rollback plan — this is what you hand a CAB or internal audit instead of a verbal explanation.

content.code:
name: promote-ai-service
on:
  push:
    tags: ['release-*']

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build immutable artifact
        run: docker build -t registry/ai-svc:${{ github.ref_name }} .
      - name: Push (untagged as env-approved yet)
        run: docker push registry/ai-svc:${{ github.ref_name }}

  eval-gate:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Run offline eval suite against golden dataset
        run: promptfoo eval --config eval/prod-gate.yaml --output eval-report.json
      - name: Fail build if quality gate not met
        run: python scripts/check_eval_thresholds.py eval-report.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: eval-evidence, path: eval-report.json }

  deploy-dev:
    needs: eval-gate
    environment: dev
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
    steps:
      - name: OIDC login to cloud
        uses: azure/login@v2
        with: { client-id: ${{ vars.DEV_CLIENT_ID }}, tenant-id: ${{ vars.TENANT_ID }} }
      - run: ./deploy.sh dev ${{ github.ref_name }}

  deploy-prod:
    needs: deploy-dev
    environment: prod   # required reviewers + wait timer configured on this environment
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read }
    steps:
      - uses: azure/login@v2
        with: { client-id: ${{ vars.PROD_CLIENT_ID }}, tenant-id: ${{ vars.TENANT_ID }} }
      - run: ./deploy.sh prod ${{ github.ref_name }}
      - name: Emit release evidence record
        run: python scripts/emit_release_evidence.py --tag ${{ github.ref_name }} --approvers "${{ github.event.deployment.creator }}"

interviewQA.q: How is a CI/CD pipeline for an AI application different from a pipeline for a normal microservice?
interviewQA.a: The application code path looks almost the same — build, test, scan, deploy — but AI adds artifacts that don't exist in a typical service: the prompt templates, the model/version pin, retrieval indexes, and guardrail configs all need their own versioning because changing any one of them changes behavior without changing a line of application code. So I add an evaluation gate — running an offline eval suite against a golden dataset — as a required check before promotion, the same way a normal pipeline requires unit tests to pass. I also treat the eval report, approver identity, and config diff as release evidence that gets archived automatically, because in a bank that evidence is what a model risk or audit reviewer asks for later, not just a green checkmark.

interviewQA.q: Walk me through how you'd design environment gating for an AI agent that has tool-calling permissions.
interviewQA.a: I'd use GitHub Environments mapped to dev/test/uat/prod, each with its own OIDC-federated cloud identity so there are no long-lived secrets sitting in the repo. Dev gets no required reviewers so engineers move fast; uat requires the eval gate to pass plus one QA sign-off; prod requires a second, different approver (segregation of duties) plus a wait timer so a bad merge can't auto-deploy at 2am. Critically, the agent's tool permissions — what systems it's allowed to call, what actions it can take autonomously — are config, versioned and reviewed like code, and I'd restrict write-scope tools to a narrower environment than read-only tools until the agent has a production track record.

interviewQA.q: What goes into your 'release evidence' for an AI change, and why does it matter for a bank specifically?
interviewQA.a: For every promotion I want: the eval report showing quality/safety scores against thresholds, the diff of what changed (prompt, model version, config), the security/dependency scan results, who approved each gate and when, and the rollback plan for that specific release. In a bank this matters because model risk management and internal audit expect the same kind of documented, repeatable process for an AI change that they'd expect for a change to a lending or fraud model — if I can't reconstruct what was live in production on a given date and who approved it, that's a control gap, not just an inconvenience.

interviewQA.q: Tell me about a time a release process you built caught a problem before it hit production.
interviewQA.a: In a past pipeline, the eval gate flagged that a prompt tweak meant to shorten responses had dropped groundedness scores below threshold on our golden dataset — the model was answering faster but hallucinating slightly more on edge-case questions. Because that gate was a required check rather than advisory, the build simply couldn't be promoted to UAT until the prompt was revised. That's the value of making evaluation a blocking gate instead of a dashboard someone checks after the fact — it turns 'we should have caught that' into 'the pipeline caught that.'

interviewQA.q: How do you handle promoting configuration changes — like a guardrail threshold or a routing rule — that aren't application code at all?
interviewQA.a: I treat them exactly like code: stored in a repo, changed via pull request, reviewed by a second person, and promoted through the same environment gates rather than edited directly in a vendor console or admin UI. That gives me a diff, a reviewer, and a rollback path for something that's otherwise invisible — config drift on guardrails is one of the easiest ways for an AI system's risk posture to silently degrade in production.

interviewQA.q: What's your approach when a business team wants to skip the eval gate because they're on a deadline?
interviewQA.a: I'd ask what specifically they're worried the gate will catch, and offer to run it in parallel with a fast-track manual review rather than skipping it outright — the point of the gate isn't bureaucracy, it's that unevaluated AI changes are exactly the kind of thing that turn into a customer-facing incident or a regulatory finding. If it's genuinely urgent, I have a documented emergency-change path with retroactive review, which is a normal pattern for regulated change management, but that path itself is logged and reviewed, not a way to routinely bypass controls.

sections.heading: LLMOps & AI Lifecycle Management
sections.summary: Covers versioning and lineage for prompts, models, and datasets, and how to make the full AI asset lifecycle auditable — this is the part of the JD that's most distinct from classic DevOps.

content.text: LLMOps extends MLOps discipline to the fact that in generative systems, the 'model' is often not something you trained — it's a third-party foundation model plus a prompt, a retrieval index, and orchestration logic, and any of those four can change independently. The operating job is to make each of them a versioned, lineage-tracked asset: a prompt is effectively code and needs the same PR review and version history as code; a model version pin (e.g., which Azure OpenAI or Bedrock model snapshot is being called) needs to be recorded per deployment so you can answer 'what generated this output' months later; and a RAG index needs a build timestamp and source-document lineage so you can reproduce or explain a retrieval. Enterprise stacks in 2026 typically layer two or three tools rather than one: MLflow (or similar) for the model/prompt registry and lifecycle where classical ML lineage already exists, plus LangSmith or Langfuse for LLM-specific tracing, prompt hubs, and version diffing.

rows: Prompt / system instructions
Immutable version snapshots with named stage labels (dev/staging/prod), stored in a prompt registry (LangSmith prompt hub, Langfuse, or MLflow 3 prompt tracking)
A prompt edit can change model behavior as much as code — reviewers need to see exactly what text was live for a given output
Model version pin
Which foundation model snapshot/version (e.g., a specific Azure OpenAI or Bedrock model version, not just 'GPT' generically) was called at inference time
Providers deprecate and silently improve model versions; you need to know precisely which version produced a decision
Retrieval index / knowledge base
Build timestamp, source document set and version, embedding model version
Explains why an answer changed even when the prompt and model didn't
Guardrail / safety config
Threshold values, blocked-topic lists, PII redaction rules, as versioned config
Regulators and internal risk teams ask what safety controls were active at a point in time
Evaluation dataset & scores
Golden dataset version plus the score each release achieved against it
Demonstrates ongoing performance monitoring, a core SR 11-7-style expectation carried into the 2026 revised interagency model risk guidance

items: Model/prompt registry: MLflow's model + prompt registry when there's existing classical-ML lineage investment; LangSmith prompt hub or Langfuse when the team is LLM-native and wants tracing built in.

Lineage question to always be able to answer: 'for this specific output, which prompt version, model version, and retrieved documents produced it?' — that's the audit trail regulators and internal model risk teams will ask for.
Model cards / release notes per version: intended use, known limitations, eval scores, and approved use cases — adapted from classical model risk documentation to generative AI.

Deprecation handling: foundation model providers retire versions on their own schedule (not yours) — lifecycle management includes a proactive re-validation process triggered before a pinned version is sunset, not a reactive scramble.

content.code:
Trace record (conceptual) for one production inference:
  request_id: 8f2a-...
  prompt_version: support-agent-v14 (approved 2026-08-02)
  model: azure-openai/gpt-x@2026-06-01-snapshot
  retrieval_index_version: kb-index-build-2026-09-20
  guardrail_config_version: pii-redaction-v3
  eval_score_at_release: groundedness 0.94, safety 0.99 (threshold 0.90/0.95)
  approver: jsmith (release r-2026-0914)
  -> this record is what you produce when a regulator or auditor asks 'why did the system say that on Sept 14'

interviewQA.q: Why treat a prompt as something that needs version control and code review, rather than just a config value?
interviewQA.a: Because a prompt is functionally the instruction set that determines model behavior — changing three words in a system prompt can shift accuracy, tone, or safety posture as much as a code change would. If it's not versioned and reviewed, you lose the ability to answer 'what changed' when behavior shifts, and you lose the audit trail a bank needs to explain a customer-facing output months later. I treat prompts like code: PR, review, immutable version snapshot, and a named stage label so I always know what's live in each environment.

interviewQA.q: How would you track lineage well enough to answer 'why did the AI say that' for a specific past interaction?
interviewQA.a: Every inference gets a trace record capturing the prompt version, the exact model version (not just the model family — providers ship silent updates), the retrieval index build and source documents if it's RAG, the guardrail config version active at the time, and which release that combination belonged to. Tools like LangSmith or Langfuse capture this automatically as tracing; if there isn't budget for a dedicated tracing platform, I'd at minimum log those four fields structured in the application's own telemetry so the reconstruction is always possible.

interviewQA.q: A foundation model provider announces they're deprecating the model version your production system pins. Walk me through your process.
interviewQA.a: First, I check how much runway there is before the deprecation date and whether the eval suite needs to be re-run against the replacement version — a 'like for like' name doesn't guarantee like-for-like behavior. I'd run the full evaluation gate against the new version on the golden dataset, compare scores against the current baseline, and treat any regression as a blocker requiring prompt or guardrail adjustment before cutover. This whole process gets scheduled proactively — ideally triggered by an automated check against the provider's deprecation calendar — rather than discovered when the old version stops responding.

interviewQA.q: What's the difference between MLflow-style lineage tracking and what LangSmith or Langfuse give you, and when would you use each?
interviewQA.a: MLflow's strength is the classical model registry and lifecycle — versioned artifacts, stage transitions, and lineage that many enterprises already standardized on for traditional ML. LangSmith and Langfuse are built LLM-native: prompt hubs with diffing, full request/response tracing including intermediate tool calls and retrieval steps, and evaluation wired directly into that trace data. In practice I've seen teams run both — MLflow for the registry and governance backbone where it already exists, layered with LangSmith or Langfuse for the LLM-specific tracing and prompt management MLflow wasn't originally built for.

interviewQA.q: How do you build a model card or equivalent documentation for a generative AI feature in a way risk teams will actually accept?
interviewQA.a: I adapt the classical model-card format — intended use, known limitations, training/grounding data description, and validation results — to generative AI's realities: instead of a single accuracy number, I document eval scores across multiple dimensions (groundedness, safety, refusal rate) against a named golden dataset version, explicitly state out-of-scope use cases, and attach the specific prompt and model version the card describes. I keep it as a living document tied to the version registry, not a one-time PDF, because generative systems change more often than a card that's revalidated annually can keep up with.

interviewQA.q: Where does lifecycle management responsibility end for you and begin for a data science or ML engineering team?
interviewQA.a: I own the operating backbone — the registry, the pipeline gates, the lineage capture, the promotion process — while the AI/ML or product team owns the actual prompt content, model selection, and evaluation criteria. The line I draw is: they decide what 'good' looks like for their use case, I make sure that decision is versioned, gated, reproducible, and auditable. That division is what lets a bank scale AI delivery across many teams without every team building its own governance from scratch.

sections.heading: Progressive Delivery for AI Services
sections.summary: Covers how to roll out a new model, prompt, or agent version with minimal blast radius using shadow traffic, canary rollout, and feature-flag-controlled exposure, plus fast rollback.

content.text: AI systems are non-deterministic — the same input can produce meaningfully different outputs across runs, so you can't rely purely on pre-release testing the way you would for deterministic code; you need production-safe ways to learn from real traffic before full exposure. The standard sequence for 2026-era LLM rollouts is: shadow mode first (duplicate real production requests to the candidate model/prompt version, log the outputs, compare against the current baseline, with zero user-facing impact), then a staged canary (10% → 25% → 50% → 75% → 100% of traffic, with automated gates at each step checking quality, latency, and cost metrics before advancing), and only then A/B testing if you're comparing genuinely different approaches rather than validating a straightforward upgrade. Feature flags — LaunchDarkly, GrowthBook, Unleash, or an internal equivalent — are the control plane that makes this practical: they let you flip which prompt version or model a given user segment sees without a redeploy, and critically, they let rollback be a config flip measured in seconds rather than a redeploy measured in minutes.

rows: Shadow
0% (mirrored, not served)
Output diff vs. baseline, latency, error rate
No user impact; manual review of diff sample
Canary wave 1
Quality/eval scores on live traffic, safety flags, latency p95
Automated: scores within threshold band for N minutes
Canary wave 2
Cost per request, token usage drift, user feedback signals (thumbs down rate)
Automated + spot manual review
Canary wave 3
Aggregate business metric (resolution rate, escalation rate)
Manual sign-off from product/risk owner
Full rollout
Sustained monitoring window before old version is decommissioned
Old version kept warm for fast rollback for an agreed window

items: Rollback readiness means the previous prompt/model/config version stays deployed and warm, and switching back is a flag flip, not a redeploy — if rollback requires a build-and-deploy cycle, it's too slow for a live incident.

Cohort consistency: for multi-turn conversations, keep a user pinned to the same model/prompt version for the duration of their session, so they don't get a mid-conversation behavior shift when a canary wave advances.

Silent degradation detection: because output quality is fuzzy, watch leading indicators (refusal rate, response length distribution shift, retrieval-empty rate) in addition to the primary eval metric — a model can look 'fine' on the headline metric while quietly degrading elsewhere.

Non-determinism budget: accept that repeated evals of the same version will show some natural variance (batching and floating-point non-associativity alone can shift results); set gate thresholds with that noise band in mind rather than treating any dip as a regression.

content.code:
Feature-flag rule sketch (GrowthBook/LaunchDarkly style):

flag: support-agent-model-version
  rule 1: if user.cohort == 'internal-testers' -> serve 'v15-candidate'
  rule 2: if user.session.assigned_variant exists -> keep serving assigned variant (cohort consistency)
  rule 3: else -> weighted rollout { v14-stable: 75%, v15-candidate: 25% }

kill-switch: on eval-alert.triggered -> force rule 'v14-stable: 100%' (rollback in seconds, no redeploy)

interviewQA.q: Why can't you just A/B test a new model version the way you'd A/B test a UI change?
interviewQA.a: Because with a UI change you know exactly what the two variants look like and the risk is bounded; with a model or prompt change, the output space is open-ended, so you want to observe behavior before it's user-facing at all. That's why I start with shadow traffic — mirror real requests to the candidate, compare outputs against the current baseline with zero user impact — before ever exposing a live user to the new version. A/B testing comes later, once shadow and early canary waves have shown the new version isn't behaviorally broken, and even then it's testing a hypothesis, not a first check for basic safety.

interviewQA.q: Describe how you'd structure a canary rollout for a new prompt version on a customer-facing support agent.
interviewQA.a: I'd shadow it first to catch anything obviously wrong, then start canary at a small percentage — say 10% — routed through a feature flag, with automated gates checking eval scores, latency, and safety flags before advancing. I'd keep a user pinned to whichever variant they started their session with, so nobody gets a jarring mid-conversation shift, and I'd watch secondary signals like refusal rate and thumbs-down rate in addition to the headline quality score, because a model can look fine on one metric while degrading somewhere else. Critically, the previous version stays warm the whole time, so if a gate fails, rollback is a flag flip, not a redeploy.

interviewQA.q: What would make you halt a canary rollout mid-way and roll back?
interviewQA.a: Any breach of a pre-agreed threshold on the automated gates — quality score drop, safety flag rate increase, latency regression, or cost per request spiking beyond expectation — should auto-halt the rollout, not wait for a person to notice. I'd also halt on a spike in user-reported negative feedback even if the automated metrics look fine, because that often catches things evals don't. The rollback itself needs to be pre-tested, not improvised — I want to know before an incident, not during one, that flipping the flag actually reverts cleanly.

interviewQA.q: How do you handle the fact that LLM outputs are non-deterministic when setting quality gate thresholds for a rollout?
interviewQA.a: I don't set thresholds as a hard pass/fail on a single run — I account for the natural variance you get from re-running the same version, which can be meaningfully wide due to things like floating-point non-associativity under batching. Gate thresholds get set with that noise band built in, and I look at trends over a sustained window rather than reacting to a single data point, otherwise you get false alarms that erode trust in the gate and people start ignoring it.

interviewQA.q: Tell me about a rollback scenario, real or how you'd handle one, involving an AI feature.
interviewQA.a: If a canary wave showed a spike in hallucinated answers on a specific question category, I wouldn't wait to diagnose the root cause before rolling back — I'd flip the feature flag back to the stable version immediately, since user impact stops the moment traffic reroutes, and investigate the root cause afterward with the shadow logs and traces already captured. That ordering — stop the bleeding first, diagnose second — is exactly why the rollback path has to be pre-built and tested, not something you engineer under pressure during the incident.

interviewQA.q: How do feature flags for AI differ from feature flags for a normal application feature?
interviewQA.a: The mechanism is the same — a flag controls what a user segment sees, and toggling it is instant — but the granularity is different: for AI I'm often flagging combinations of prompt version, model version, and retrieval config together as a single 'variant,' not just an on/off switch, and I need session-level stickiness so a single conversation doesn't straddle two variants. I also wire the flag's kill-switch directly to the evaluation and observability alerting, so a quality regression detected automatically can trigger the rollback without a human in the loop for the first response.

sections.heading: Evaluation, Observability & Production Readiness
sections.summary: Covers building quality gates, telemetry, dashboards, and runbooks so an AI service is measurable and supportable in production, not just impressive in a demo.

content.text: The mature pattern here is two complementary tool categories, not one: a lightweight evaluation framework that lives in the repo and runs in CI as a quality gate (DeepEval, Ragas for RAG-specific checks, or Promptfoo, often also used for red-teaming), and a production observability platform that lives in the running system and captures live traces, human annotation, and regression tracking (LangSmith, Langfuse, or Arize Phoenix, generally built on OpenTelemetry/OpenInference conventions). The distinction matters operationally: the eval framework blocks a bad release before it ships; the observability platform tells you what's actually happening to real users afterward, including things no offline eval anticipated. Production readiness for an AI service means having both, plus the same operational basics any production service needs — dashboards a support engineer can read without an AI background, runbooks for the failure modes specific to AI (degraded groundedness, retrieval failures, upstream model provider outage, cost spike), and a documented go-live checklist that a release can't pass without.

rows: Offline eval / CI gate
DeepEval, Ragas, Promptfoo
Does this candidate version meet the quality/safety bar before it ships?
Live tracing & observability
LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix (OpenTelemetry/OpenInference-based)
What actually happened on this specific production request — prompt, retrieval, tool calls, latency, tokens?
Metrics & alerting
Grafana/Datadog dashboards fed by the above, plus infra metrics
Is the service healthy right now — latency, error rate, refusal rate, cost per request?
Human review loop
Annotation queues in the observability platform
Are the automated eval scores still correlated with what a human would judge good?

items: Quality gates to enforce pre-release: groundedness/faithfulness (for RAG), toxicity/safety score, refusal-rate sanity check, and a regression check against the previous version's scores on the same golden dataset.

Production telemetry to always capture: tokens in/out per request, latency (including time-to-first-token for streaming), retrieval hit/miss rate, tool-call success/failure, and a sampled log of full traces for human review.

Dashboards built for two audiences: an ops/support dashboard (is it up, is it slow, is it expensive) and a quality dashboard (is it still accurate, what's the trend on user feedback signals) — conflating the two makes neither useful.

Runbooks specific to AI failure modes: upstream model provider degraded/outage (fallback model or graceful degradation message), retrieval index stale or empty, sudden token-cost spike (possible prompt injection or loop), and quality score alert triggered by the eval pipeline post-deploy.

Production-readiness checklist as a hard gate: eval thresholds met, rollback tested, dashboards live, on-call runbook written, cost alert configured, and a named owner — no go-live without all boxes checked.

content.code:
# production readiness checklist (excerpt, enforced as a PR template / release gate)
readiness_checklist:
  - eval_thresholds_met: true          # from CI eval-gate job
  - rollback_tested_in_last_30_days: true
  - dashboards:
      ops_dashboard_linked: true
      quality_dashboard_linked: true
  - runbooks:
      upstream_outage: linked
      cost_spike: linked
      quality_regression_alert: linked
  - cost_alert_configured: true        # token spend anomaly threshold set
  - named_on_call_owner: required
  - blocking: any_false -> release cannot proceed to prod environment

interviewQA.q: What's the difference between an evaluation framework and an observability platform, and why do you need both?
interviewQA.a: The evaluation framework — something like DeepEval or Ragas — runs in CI against a fixed golden dataset and gives you a pass/fail gate before a release ships; it's fast, repeatable, and catches known failure modes. The observability platform — LangSmith, Langfuse, or Arize Phoenix — captures what's actually happening to real production traffic, including failure modes you never anticipated in your golden dataset. I need both because offline eval alone gives false confidence — real users ask things your test set didn't cover — and observability alone is reactive, catching problems only after they've already shipped.

interviewQA.q: What telemetry do you consider non-negotiable for an AI service in production?
interviewQA.a: Tokens in and out per request, so cost is traceable; latency including time-to-first-token if it's streaming; retrieval hit/miss rate for RAG systems, because a silent retrieval failure often looks like a hallucination but is actually a data problem; tool-call success and failure rates for agents; and a sampled full trace log for human review, since aggregate metrics alone can hide a specific bad pattern. Without these, an incident becomes guesswork instead of investigation.

interviewQA.q: How would you design a runbook for 'the upstream model provider is degraded or down'?
interviewQA.a: First, detection — an alert on elevated latency or error rate specifically from the provider API, distinct from our own service errors. Then a documented decision tree: is there an approved fallback model to route to via the same feature-flag mechanism used for rollouts, or does the service degrade gracefully with a clear user-facing message instead of a raw error? I'd also make sure the runbook specifies who gets paged, what the customer communication is, and how we detect the provider has recovered before flipping back — this is exactly the kind of failure mode that's unique to depending on a third-party foundation model versus your own infrastructure.

interviewQA.q: How do you keep automated eval scores honest — how do you know they still correlate with what a human would actually judge as good?
interviewQA.a: I build in a periodic human annotation loop — sampling live production traces into a review queue, generally something the observability platform supports natively — and compare human judgments against the automated scores on the same samples. If they start diverging, that's a signal the golden dataset or the eval metric itself has gone stale relative to how the product or user base has evolved, and it needs to be refreshed rather than trusted blindly.

interviewQA.q: What would you put on a production-readiness checklist before letting a team's AI feature go live, and why make it a hard gate rather than a suggestion?
interviewQA.a: Eval thresholds met, rollback tested within a recent window, both an ops dashboard and a quality dashboard linked and live, runbooks written for the AI-specific failure modes, a cost alert configured, and a named on-call owner. I make it a hard, enforced gate rather than a checklist people eyeball because 'we'll add monitoring after launch' is exactly how you end up with an AI incident nobody can diagnose — the whole point of a paved road is that teams can't accidentally skip the parts that matter under deadline pressure.

interviewQA.q: A dashboard shows cost per request has tripled overnight with no deployment. How do you investigate?
interviewQA.a: I'd first check the trace-level telemetry for a shift in token counts — is input growing (longer conversations, a retrieval bug pulling in too much context) or output growing (the model looping, or a prompt change causing longer responses)? I'd also check for a spike in request volume versus a spike in per-request cost, since those point to very different causes, and I'd specifically check for anything that looks like prompt injection or an agent stuck in a retry loop, since runaway tool-calling loops are a real and costly AI-specific failure mode that a traditional service wouldn't have.

sections.heading: AI FinOps & Capacity Governance
sections.summary: Covers giving the organization visibility into token spend, managing quota/rate limits across providers, attributing cost to teams, and finding optimization opportunities before finance does.

content.text: AI FinOps is a reconciliation problem before it's an optimization problem: a bank running workloads across Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, and possibly other providers gets separate bills in different units on different cycles, and when a developer calls a model API directly there's often no built-in way to attribute that cost to a team, product, or cost center. The foundational control is disciplined API key or identity structure — one key/principal per team or application, provisioned only with a named owner and an approved use case — layered with provider-native cost-allocation features (AWS Bedrock's Application Inference Profiles and Bedrock Projects push tags into the Cost and Usage Report at the inference-call level; Azure OpenAI equivalents tag by resource and deployment). On top of attribution sits capacity governance: quota and rate-limit management so one team's traffic spike can't starve another's, and Provisioned Throughput Unit (PTU) utilization tracking so reserved capacity isn't sitting idle while another team throttles on shared capacity.

items: Attribution mechanism: one API key or cloud identity per team/application, tagged with cost center at provisioning time — never a shared key across multiple teams, which makes chargeback guesswork.

Provider-native tools: AWS Bedrock Application Inference Profiles and Bedrock Projects for per-call cost tagging; Azure OpenAI deployment-level tagging and Cost Management + PTU utilization reporting.
Quota governance: pre-approved per-team rate limits/quotas so a runaway agent loop or a traffic spike in one product can't exhaust shared capacity and throttle every other team on the platform.

Optimization levers, roughly in order of effort: prompt/context trimming and caching, routing simple requests to a smaller/cheaper model (model tiering), batching where latency allows, and renegotiating reserved-capacity (PTU) sizing against actual utilization trends.

Showback/chargeback cadence: a monthly (or more frequent) cost-by-team report that product owners actually see, so cost becomes a design input for their AI feature roadmap rather than a surprise finance escalation.

interviewQA.q: A bank is running AI workloads across Azure OpenAI and AWS Bedrock. How do you give finance an accurate view of who's spending what?
interviewQA.a: I start with attribution at the point of provisioning — every team or application gets its own API key or cloud identity, never a shared one, tagged with a cost center up front, because you can't retroactively reconstruct attribution from a shared key's traffic. Then I use each provider's native tagging — Bedrock's Application Inference Profiles and Bedrock Projects push cost data at the inference-call level, Azure OpenAI has equivalent deployment-level tagging — and roll both into a single normalized cost-by-team dashboard, since the two providers bill in different units and cycles and finance shouldn't have to reconcile that manually.

interviewQA.q: What's the difference between cost per inference and token efficiency ratio, and why track both?
interviewQA.a: Cost per inference tells you the unit economics of a feature — is a single resolved conversation or request cheap enough to be viable at scale. Token efficiency ratio tells you whether you're being wasteful getting there — how much of what you're paying for is actually useful output versus bloated context or redundant retries. A feature can have an acceptable cost-per-inference while still being token-inefficient, and that's usually your first, cheapest optimization lever — trimming context or caching — before you'd ever consider a more disruptive change like switching models.

interviewQA.q: How do you manage quota and rate limits so one team's AI feature doesn't starve another team's on shared platform capacity?
interviewQA.a: I set pre-approved per-team quotas as part of onboarding onto the platform, sized against expected usage, rather than letting every team hit a shared limit unconstrained. I also track quota utilization against the ceiling continuously so I can see a team approaching its limit before it starts throttling, and I build in request queuing or backoff for non-urgent workloads so a spike degrades gracefully instead of hard-failing. For genuinely urgent capacity needs, there's a fast-track process to request a quota increase rather than a team silently working around the limit.

interviewQA.q: When would you recommend Provisioned Throughput / reserved capacity versus pay-as-you-go, and how do you know if a PTU reservation is sized correctly?
interviewQA.a: Reserved capacity makes sense for predictable, high-volume, latency-sensitive workloads where pay-as-you-go throttling risk is unacceptable; pay-as-you-go fits spiky or low-volume workloads where you'd otherwise pay for idle reserved capacity. I judge sizing by tracking PTU utilization over time — consistently near 100% utilization with regular overflow to pay-as-you-go means the reservation is undersized, while sustained low utilization means the bank is paying for capacity nobody's using, and either signal should trigger a resizing conversation, not just get absorbed silently into the budget.

interviewQA.q: Describe a cost optimization you'd pursue first for an AI feature that's more expensive than expected, versus one you'd hold off on.
interviewQA.a: First and cheapest: audit for prompt/context bloat and unnecessary repeated context that could be cached or trimmed, since that's often pure waste with no behavior change. Next: model tiering — routing simple, high-volume requests to a smaller/cheaper model and reserving the frontier model for genuinely complex requests. I'd hold off on renegotiating reserved-capacity sizing or making architectural changes until I had utilization data over a meaningful window, because reacting to a single expensive week with a structural change is how you end up either over-correcting or locking in the wrong capacity commitment.

interviewQA.q: How do you make cost visibility something product teams actually act on, rather than a report finance reads once a quarter?
interviewQA.a: I push a cost-by-team dashboard to the same place engineering already looks — tied into the release and observability tooling, not a separate finance-only report — and make it frequent enough (I'd aim for near-real-time, or at minimum weekly) that a team sees the cost impact of a change close to when they made it. I've also found it helps to surface a 'top 10 most expensive request patterns' view specifically for engineering, because that turns an abstract budget number into a concrete, fixable list of optimization targets a team can actually act on.

sections.heading: How to Talk About Your Experience — Cross-Functional & Behavioral
sections.summary: This role lives at the intersection of platform engineering, QA/SRE, security, architecture, and product — interviewers will probe whether you can operate across those boundaries in a regulated environment without becoming either a bottleneck or a rubber stamp.

content.text: Because this is a newer role category, interviewers often can't benchmark you against a long list of people who've done exactly this before — so they lean harder on behavioral questions to assess judgment: do you default to control or to enablement, do you know when to escalate versus decide yourself, and can you explain a technical tradeoff to a non-technical risk or audit stakeholder. The strongest frame for a banking context is 'paved road, not roadblock' — you're building standard patterns that let teams move fast inside guardrails, and your credibility comes from being the person who makes releases safer and faster at the same time, not slower. It also helps to be current and honest about the regulatory landscape: the April 2026 revised interagency model risk management guidance from the Fed/FDIC/OCC explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from its scope pending a future request-for-information — meaning banks right now are largely building their own interim internal governance for gen AI rather than following a settled external standard, and a candidate who can speak to that gap intelligently stands out.

items: Frame your CI/CD and cloud-native production experience as the foundation, and your AI-specific knowledge as the extension — most interviewers are more reassured by strong fundamentals plus demonstrated ability to learn the AI-specific layer than by AI buzzwords without operational depth.

Have one detailed story ready for each of: a release you gated that prevented a bad deploy, an incident you helped resolve (ideally with a rollback), a cost anomaly you caught, and a cross-team disagreement you navigated (e.g., security wanted to block something, product wanted to ship it).

Be ready to explain a technical concept (e.g., why shadow traffic matters) to a hypothetical non-technical stakeholder in one or two sentences — this is a common banking-interview move to test communication, not just knowledge.

Know the current regulatory gap: gen AI/agentic AI is explicitly out of scope of the 2026 revised interagency model risk guidance, with an RFI promised — meaning internal governance you help build is currently the primary control, not a stopgap until regulation catches up.

interviewQA.q: How do you balance moving fast for AI product teams with the control requirements of a bank?
interviewQA.a: My approach is to put the controls into the paved road itself, so following the standard path is the fastest way to ship, not the slowest — if the eval gate, the promotion pipeline, and the rollback mechanism are all pre-built and self-service, teams don't experience governance as friction, they experience it as infrastructure. Where I do slow things down deliberately is anything touching customer-facing risk or an irreversible action, and I'm upfront with product teams about why that specific gate exists rather than applying blanket caution everywhere, which is what actually erodes trust in a governance function.

interviewQA.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a security or architecture team's requirement and how you handled it.
interviewQA.a: I'd walk through a specific case where I thought a proposed control was disproportionate to the actual risk — say, a security requirement that would have added a manual approval step for low-risk, read-only agent actions the same as for high-risk write actions. I brought data — the actual blast radius and reversibility of the read-only case — rather than just an opinion, proposed a tiered control instead of a blanket one, and let the security team make the final call with that information, because they own that risk decision even when I'm the one who has to operationalize it. The resolution matters less than showing I escalate with evidence rather than either rolling over or unilaterally overriding a control.

interviewQA.q: How would you explain to a non-technical risk committee why you're rolling out a new model version gradually instead of all at once?
interviewQA.a: I'd say something like: 'AI models don't behave identically to how they tested in the lab once they see real customer questions, so instead of switching everyone over at once, we show the new version to a small slice of traffic first, watch it closely, and only expand once we're confident — and if anything looks wrong, we can switch everyone back in seconds, not hours.' That framing — small exposure, close watching, instant reversibility — tends to land well with a risk-oriented audience because it maps directly onto concepts they already use for other kinds of change control.

interviewQA.q: Model risk management guidance for generative AI is still evolving — the 2026 interagency guidance explicitly doesn't cover it yet. How does that affect how you operate?
interviewQA.a: It means I can't lean on an established external standard the way a classical model risk team can point to SR 11-7-style expectations — I have to help build the bank's interim internal governance discipline proactively, borrowing the spirit of established model risk practices (independent validation, ongoing monitoring, documented approval) and adapting them to generative and agentic AI's specifics, like non-deterministic outputs and prompt-level change management. I'd also stay alert to the promised regulatory request-for-information, because when that lands, whatever internal framework I've built needs to be able to map onto it without a total rebuild — so I try to over-document now rather than assume today's informal process is permanent.

interviewQA.q: Describe how you'd onboard a new AI product team onto your release and operational standards without becoming a bottleneck yourself.
interviewQA.a: I'd give them self-service templates — a pipeline skeleton, an eval-gate config, a dashboard template, a runbook template — so they can adopt the pattern without needing me in the loop for every step, and I'd document the 'why' behind each control so they can make sound judgment calls on edge cases rather than escalating everything to me. My own time then goes to the harder cases — genuinely novel architectures, edge-case risk questions — rather than repeatedly answering the same onboarding questions, which is really the definition of a paved road versus a gatekeeper model.

interviewQA.q: What would you do in your first 90 days in this role at a bank building out its AI Center of Excellence?
interviewQA.a: I'd start by mapping what's already shipping — which teams have AI features in production today and what, if any, release/observability/cost discipline already exists — because there's likely already tribal knowledge and partial tooling I shouldn't bulldoze. Then I'd pick one or two live teams to co-build the first version of the paved road with, rather than designing it in isolation, so the templates are shaped by a real workload before I generalize them. By day 90 I'd want at least one team through a full gated promotion pipeline with real evaluation, observability, and cost dashboards live, plus a documented readiness checklist I can start socializing with platform engineering, QA/SRE, security, and the model risk function as the emerging standard.
